25-001.r: Polo (Chaugan) introduced in India → Turks; Qutbuddin Aybak loved it and died in 1210 while playing it.

25-002.r: Firuz Tughluq → construction of canals; Balban → Nawruz; Alauddin → Diwan-i-Riyasat; Jahangir → Sir Thomas Roe (British envoy).

25-003.r: Hindu gods and goddesses worshipped in royal palaces → under Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah, who took the throne after Mubarak Shah's assassination.

25-004.r: Wrong pair: Hamida Banu Begum–wife of Alauddin Khilji; she was Humayun's queen and Akbar's mother. Correct: Iltutmish–Raziyya's father; Gulbadan–Babur's daughter; Shah Turkan–Iltutmish's wife.

25-005.r: Wrong pair: Abdur Razzaq–Turkey; he was an Iranian envoy (to Deva Raya II, 1422-46 AD). Correct: Ibn Battuta–Morocco; Marco Polo–Italy (Venice); Nuniz–Portugal.

25-006.r: Arrival order: Al-Biruni (with Mahmud Ghazni) → Ibn Battuta (1333-1342) → Tavernier (French, 17th century, Shahjahan) → Manucci (Italian, 1653-1708).

25-007.r: 'Dastar-Bandan' → Ulema (senior religious and judicial officials), named for their official turban.

25-008.t: Don't mix: Dastar-Bandan (turban) = Ulema; Kulah-Daran (cap) = Sayyids.

25-009.r: Earliest reference to the magnetic compass in Indian seas → Sadiduddin Muhammad 'Aufi', in Jawami-ul-Hikayat (also wrote Lubab-ul-Albab).

25-010.r: Order: Raziyya Sultan (1236-1240) → Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) → Sher Shah (1540-1545) → Akbar (1556-1605).

25-011.r: Battle of Chandawar → 1194; Taimur's attack → 1398; Battle of Talikota → 1565; Battle of Ghaghra → 1529.

25-012.r: Wrong pair: Chand Bibi–Oudh; she was regent of Bijapur and Ahmednagar (daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah I). Correct: Bahadur Shah–Gujarat; Raziyya–Delhi; Baz Bahadur–Malwa.

25-013.r: Order: Qutub Minar (Aybak, Iltutmish) → Firuz Tughluq's death (1388) → Portuguese arrival, Vasco-da-Gama (1498) → Krishnadeva Raya's reign (1509-1529).

25-014.r: Order: Second Tarain (1192) → Jalaluddin Khalji murdered (1296) → Afghanpur conspiracy (Ghiyasuddin's death; Ulugh Khan accused) → Muhammad Tughluq's capital transfer.

25-015.r: Greatest premodern traveller (about 44 countries, 73,000 miles, 30 years) → Ibn Battuta; Marco Polo covered about 24000 miles over 24 years from 1271.

25-016.r: Correct: Mahendravarman–Mattavilasaprahasana. Krishnadeva Raya → Amuktamalyada; Bhoja → Samaranganasutradhar; Somesvara → Manasollasa.

25-017.r: Shortest-ruling Delhi Sultanate dynasty → Khalji (1290-1320 AD).

25-018.r: Longest reign of these → Bahlol Lodi (1451-1489); Alauddin Khalji 1296-1316, Muhammad bin Tughlaq 1325-1351, Balban 1266-1286.

25-019.r: Sayyid order: Khizr Khan (1414-1421) → Mubarak Shah (1421-1434) → Muhammad Shah (1434-1445) → Ala-ud-Din Alam Shah (1445-1451).

25-020.r: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani did not serve Iltutmish; served Alauddin Khilji (won Malwa, 1305 AD), Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Tughlaq.

25-021.r: Started in the Rajput period → Jauhar, Rajput women's mass self-immolation to escape capture during Muslim invasions.

25-022.r: Jain scholar among these → Hemchandra Suri, prominent in the Solanki court of Jai Singh Siddharaj.

25-023.r: Plassey → 1757 AD; Kalinga → 261 BC; Haldighati → 1576 AD; (Second) Tarain → 1192 AD.

25-024.r: Akbar → Ain-i-Dahsala; Muhammad Tughluq → token currency; Iltutmish → Chahalgani (the Forty) nobles; Sher Shah → Sadak-i-Azam (Sonargaon to Lahore).

25-026.r: 'Fanam' in medieval India → small gold coins of South India (used up to the 19th century).

25-027.r: Not grown by Indian peasants in the 13th-14th centuries → maize (brought later by the Portuguese); Ibn Battuta notes rice, wheat, sugarcane, cotton.
25-027.t: Wheat, barley and gram are old Indian crops; maize is a New World crop.

25-028.r: 'Mahattara' and 'Pattakila' → village headmen (Pattakila in Maharashtra, Mahattaka in Uttar Pradesh); H.C. Verma calls Mahattar a head of artisans.

26-001.r: Jaunpur → founded by Firuz Shah Tughluq in memory of cousin Muhammad-bin-Tughluq (Jauna Khan); governor Malik Sarwar later founded the Sharqi dynasty.

26-003.r: 'Shiraz of East' / 'Shiraz-i-Hind' → Jaunpur, at its peak under Sharqi ruler Ibrahim Shah (1402-1440 AD), who built in the Sharqi style.

26-005.r: Last ruler of Jaunpur → Hussain Shah, defeated by Bahlul Lodi; Malik Sarwar made Jaunpur independent in 1394 AD.

26-006.r: A and R true, R explains A: Jaunpur was called Shiraz-i-Hind because it was a great centre of learning under the Sharqis (Ibrahim Shah Sharqi).

26-007.r: 'Akbar of Kashmir' → Zain-ul-Abidin (Shahi Khan, from 1420 AD); first to abolish Jizya and ban cow slaughter; Mahabharata, Rajatarangini put into Persian.

26-010.r: Jama Masjid, Kashmir (built by Sikandar Butshikan, 1400 AD; expanded by Zain-ul-Abidin) → turrets, Buddhist pagoda-like look, Persian style (all three).

26-011.r: Not in Rana Kumbha's court → Muni Jin Vijay Suri (Akbar's court, per book); Muni Sunder Suri, Natha and Tilla Bhatt were Kumbha's scholars.

26-012.r: Wrong pair: Malik Sarwar (Khwaja Jahan)–Malwa; he founded the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur (1394 AD). Correct: Rana Hamir–Mewar; Rana Chunda–Marwar; Malik Raja Farooqi–Khandesh.

26-013.r: Only Durgara–Jammu is correct; Champaka (Chamba) and Kuluta (Kullu) are in present Himachal Pradesh, not Central India or Malabar.

26-014.r: Bahmani kingdom founded → Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu, Zafar Khan), 1347 AD; first capital Gulbarga (renamed Hasanabad).

26-019.r: Bahmani kingdom founded → 14th century A.D. (1347), by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah.

26-020.r: Adil Shahi → Bijapur (Yusuf Adil Shah); Qutb Shahi → Golconda (Quli Qutb Shah); Nizam Shahi → Ahmadnagar (Malik Ahmad); Sharqi → Jaunpur (Malik Sarwar).
26-020.h: A-B, Q-G, N-A: Adil-Bijapur, Qutb-Golconda, Nizam-Ahmadnagar.

26-021.r: Muslim ruler hailed as 'Jagadguru' → Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur; tolerant; founded Nauraspur; wrote Kitab-i-Nauras (nine rasas).

26-022.r: Kitab-i-Nauras → Ibrahim Adil Shah II, ruler of Bijapur, in the Deccani language.

26-023.r: Nizam Shahi Ahmadnagar ended → annexed by Shahjahan (1632); Hussain Nizam Shah III jailed for life at Gwalior; Daulatabad fort got by a 10.5 lakh bribe to Fateh Khan.

26-024.r: Wrong pair: Yusuf Adil Shah–Ahmadnagar; he ruled Bijapur. Correct: Baz Bahadur–Malwa; Qutb Shah–Golconda; Sultan Muzaffar Shah–Gujarat.

26-025.r: Golconda → now in Hyderabad; Qutb Shahi capital (16th-17th century), ended by Aurangzeb; famous for diamonds.

26-026.r: Gujarat ruler who let the Portuguese have Diu → Bahadur Shah, by a 1535 AD treaty with Nuno da Cunha for help against the Mughals.

26-027.r: Correct: Hoysala–Dwarasamudra (and Pandya–Madurai). Wrong: Kakatiya capital Warangal, Yadava capital Devgiri (options swapped them).
26-027.c: Book says both (b) and (d) are correct.

26-029.r: None began in the early eighth century: Hoysala (10th-14th century), Gahadavala (11th-12th), Kakatiya (12th-14th), Yadava of Devagiri (later medieval).

26-030.r: Capitals: Pallava → Kanchi; Pandya → Madura; Yadava → Devagiri; Kakatiya → Warangal.

26-031.r: Female king Rudrama Devi → Kakatiya dynasty; ruled because her father Ganapati had no son.

26-032.r: Both true: Rudrama (daughter of Ganapati Dev) was the fourth independent Kakatiya ruler of Warangal; defeated Pandyas, Eastern Gangas of Orissa and Seunas of Devagiri.

26-033.r: Hoysala monuments → Halebidu (Hoysaleshvara temple, Shiva) and Belur (Chennakeshava temple), Karnataka.
26-033.t: Don't pick Hampi; Hampi is Vijayanagara, not Hoysala.

26-034.r: Hoysala capital Dwarasamudra → modern Halebidu (Hassan district, Karnataka).

26-035.r: One of the world's largest domes → Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur, the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah.
